name: a Polish of a 650-word email
input:
Hi everyone,

I wanted to send a proper write-up after Thursday's call, because a few of you joined late and I think we left some things more open than they really are. This is long, sorry. The short version is that the billing migration is moving from October 14 to October 28, and the reason is the tax export, not the payment provider.

Here is what happened. When Priya Raman ran the dry run against the staging copy of the ledger last Tuesday, the invoices came through fine, the refunds came through fine, but the VAT export for our German and Austrian customers produced totals that were off by a few cents on roughly 3% of rows. A few cents does not sound like much, but our accountants at Hollis & Vane file those numbers directly, and they told us very clearly that they will not accept a mismatch of any size. Priya traced it to rounding. The old system rounds each line item and then sums; Stripe Billing sums and then rounds. Both are defensible, but we have to pick one and document it before anything goes live.

So the plan is this. Priya will write a small reconciliation script that compares both methods on the last twelve months of invoices and flags every row where they disagree. She expects that to be ready by Friday, October 10. Tomasz Wiśniewski will take the output to Hollis & Vane on Monday, October 13, and get a written answer on which method they want us to use going forward. If they choose the Stripe behavior, we do nothing except update the export notes. If they choose ours, Daniel will add a rounding adapter in the export job, which he estimates at two days of work plus a day of testing.

The cutover itself stays the same as before. We freeze plan changes at 18:00 CET on the Friday before, run the final sync overnight, and switch the checkout over on Saturday morning. The runbook lives at https://wiki.northfield.io/billing/cutover-runbook and the rollback steps are at the bottom of that page. Please read the rollback section even if you think you know it, because Daniel rewrote it last week after the load test and two of the steps changed order.

A few smaller items that came up:

Customer support needs the new invoice PDF template before the switch, not after. Hannah Okafor asked for at least a week to update the help center articles and the canned replies. I have promised her the final template by October 20. The draft is in the shared drive under Billing / Templates / invoice-v3-draft.pdf.

The finance dashboard will show duplicate revenue for the migration weekend, because both systems will report the same transactions for about thirty-six hours. Jonas has a filter ready that hides the old source after the switch. Nobody needs to panic about that spike on Monday morning.

We still do not have a decision on whether to migrate the 412 legacy annual plans or leave them on the old system until they renew. My recommendation is to leave them. Moving them means prorating, and prorating is exactly where the rounding problem bites hardest. If anyone disagrees, please reply to this thread by Wednesday so we can settle it in the next call.

Finally, the status page. Marketing wants to announce the switch to customers, but I would rather we say nothing until it is done and stable. A billing change is invisible when it works, and announcing it only invites people to look for problems. Sofia, can you and I talk about this on Tuesday? Fifteen minutes is enough.

The next sync is Thursday, October 16, at 10:30 CET, same link as always: https://meet.northfield.io/billing-weekly. If the accountants have answered by then, that call will be short.

Thanks, all. This has been a slog, and I appreciate how carefully everyone has handled it.

Marta

name: a Polish of a 630-word letter
input:
Dear Aunt Lucy,

I have owed you a real letter since the summer, and your postcard from Lisbon finally shamed me into writing one. Thank you for it. The picture of the yellow tram is now on our fridge, and Oskar asks every morning whether we can go and ride it. I told him maybe when he is bigger, and he said he is already bigger than last week, which is true, so I may have to think of a better answer.

So much has happened since we last talked properly. We moved at the end of June, as you know, but I don't think I ever told you what the new place is actually like. It is the ground floor of an old brick house on a quiet street near the river. The kitchen is small and the windows stick when it rains, but there is a garden, a real one, with an apple tree that nobody has pruned in years and a shed full of rusty tools that the previous owner simply left behind. Ben spent most of August clearing it out. He found a box of letters from the 1960s under the floorboards, written by a woman called Edith to her sister in Leeds. We have not decided what to do with them yet. It feels wrong to read them and wrong to throw them away.

Work is calmer than it was. The library finally hired a second children's librarian, so I no longer run every story hour myself. Her name is Grace and she does voices far better than I do. On Tuesdays I now run a small reading group for older people instead, mostly retired teachers and one former ship's engineer who has opinions about every novel that mentions the sea. Last month we read a book about a lighthouse keeper and he spent forty minutes explaining why the author got the lamp mechanism wrong. It was the best meeting we have had.

Oskar started nursery in September. The first week was hard. He cried at the gate every morning and I cried in the car afterwards. By the third week he was running in without looking back, which was its own kind of hard. He has a best friend now, a very serious girl called Nell who has decided that she is a cat. Oskar is allowed to be a cat too, but only a small one.

Mum is doing better than she was in the spring. The new medication seems to be working, and she has started walking to the shops again on her own. She still refuses to use the stick the doctor gave her, but she carries it, which I suppose is progress. She asks about you often. I think a phone call from you would cheer her up more than anything I could say. Sundays after lunch are the best time.

Now, the real reason for this letter. We would love you to come and stay at Christmas. The spare room is tiny, but the bed is good, and the garden will be bare by then but the apple tree looks lovely in frost. Ben has promised to make his mother's red cabbage, and I will try the gingerbread recipe you sent me years ago, the one with the black pepper. No pressure at all. If the journey is too much, we would happily drive up to you in the new year instead.

Write back when you can, or call. I miss our long talks at your kitchen table, the ones that started at breakfast and somehow ended at dinner.

With all my love,
Anna

P.S. Oskar has drawn you a picture of the tram. It is purple, because he says yellow is boring. It is in the envelope.

name: a Polish of an 890-word dictation
input:
Okay so this is going to be kind of a brain dump about the conference trip because I need to get it out of my head before I forget all of it, and I'll clean it up later for the team. So, um, the conference was in Porto, it was three days, the fourteenth to the sixteenth, and honestly it was better than I expected, I went in thinking it would be mostly vendor talks and it was actually maybe half that, which for this kind of event is pretty good.

The first day was the one I was most excited about, because the keynote was Helena Varga, who wrote the book on event sourcing that we basically used as a manual when we rebuilt the order service. And her talk was, I mean it was good, but it wasn't what I expected. She spent most of it saying that she regrets some of what she wrote, that a lot of teams adopted event sourcing for systems that did not need it, and that the operational cost is way higher than people think. Which, yeah. That's us. That's exactly us. Like, I sat there thinking about the replay job that takes nine hours and nobody wants to touch. She said the one test she uses now is whether the business actually asks questions about history, like what did this look like on a given date, and if they don't, you probably just want a normal database with an audit table. I want to bring that to our architecture review, maybe not as a "we were wrong" thing but more as, let's check whether the order service still needs this or whether it was the right call at the time and isn't anymore.

Then there was a, wait, no, that was day two. Okay, day one afternoon I went to two talks on observability, one was fine, one was really good. The good one was by a guy from a Danish logistics company, I think his name was Mikkel something, I have it written down somewhere. His team cut their logging bill by about seventy percent by dropping most debug logs in production and sampling the rest, and putting the money into tracing instead. The thing that stuck with me was that he said nobody on his team had read a debug log in production in over a year, they just searched traces. I don't think we're there, but I bet we're closer than we think, and our log bill is, what, the third biggest line in the cloud budget? Something like that. Worth asking Priyanka for the actual number.

Day two was workshops. I did the one on contract testing, which was hands-on, we used Pact, and I have to admit I came out more convinced than I went in. We have that recurring problem where the mobile team ships against an API shape that the backend changed two weeks ago, and contract tests would have caught every single one of those, I'm pretty sure. The setup isn't trivial though. You need a broker, you need both sides to actually publish, and the person running it said the biggest failure mode is teams that set it up and then stop updating the contracts, so they slowly drift into being useless. So if we do this it needs an owner. Maybe Ahmed? He's been complaining about this exact problem for months, so he might actually want it.

The evening of day two there was a dinner thing, which I almost skipped because I was tired, but I'm glad I went because I ended up sitting next to two people from a fintech in Kraków who are doing almost exactly the migration we're planning, moving off the old message queue onto Kafka. They're about six months ahead of us. They offered to do a call with our team and walk through what went wrong, which, I mean that's incredibly useful, people never write the honest version of that in blog posts. I have their emails. I'll set something up for next month.

Day three I was honestly a bit burnt out. I went to one talk on platform teams that was mostly a sales pitch, left halfway through, and spent the rest of the morning in the hallway talking to people, which, as everyone always says, is the actual conference. I had a long chat with someone who runs developer experience at a gaming company, and she said the single best thing they did was measure how long it takes a new hire to ship their first change to production, and treat that number like a product metric. Theirs went from eleven days to two. I have no idea what ours is. Probably bad. I'd love to find out.

So, takeaways, let me try to actually list them. One, look again at whether the order service needs event sourcing. Two, get the real logging cost and see if we can shift some of it to tracing. Three, pilot contract testing between mobile and the orders API, with an owner, maybe Ahmed. Four, set up the call with the Kraków team before we start the Kafka migration. Five, measure time to first production change for new hires. That's it, that's the list. I'll turn this into something readable before Friday's team meeting.

The conference was in Porto, running from the fourteenth to the sixteenth. I expected mostly vendor talks, but it was closer to half that, which is good for this type of event.

Day one featured a keynote by Helena Varga, who wrote the book on event sourcing we used as a manual for rebuilding the order service. Her talk was insightful but unexpected. She expressed regret about some of her writing, noting that many teams adopted event sourcing for systems that didn't need it and that the operational cost is higher than anticipated. She suggested that if a business does not ask questions about history (what the state looked like on a given date), a normal database with an audit table is preferable. I plan to bring this up in our architecture review to assess whether the order service still needs event sourcing or if it was the right initial decision.

The afternoon of day one included two talks on observability. One was fine, but the other, by a representative from a Danish logistics company (Mikkel something), was excellent. His team cut their logging bill by about seventy percent by dropping most debug logs in production and sampling the rest, redirecting the savings to tracing. He noted that his team members had not read a debug log in production in over a year, relying instead on traces. We should investigate our logging costs; I will ask Priyanka for the actual figure to see if we can shift resources to tracing, as our log bill is likely the third biggest line in the cloud budget.

Day two involved workshops. I attended a hands-on session on contract testing using Pact. I left more convinced than when I started. We face a recurring issue where the mobile team ships against an API shape that the backend changed recently, which contract tests should have caught. However, the setup is complex, requiring a broker and both sides to publish. The facilitator noted that the biggest failure mode is teams setting up the system and then failing to update the contracts, causing them to become useless. This initiative needs an owner; Ahmed has been complaining about this exact problem, so he might be interested.

That evening, I attended a dinner. I was glad to go because I sat next to two people from a fintech in Kraków who are planning a migration from the old message queue to Kafka, about six months ahead of us. They offered to schedule a call for our team to review what went wrong, which is incredibly useful. I have their emails and will set something up for next month.

Day three was draining. I attended a talk on platform teams that was mostly a sales pitch and left halfway through. I spent the rest of the morning networking. I had a long conversation with someone who manages developer experience at a gaming company. She stated their best practice was measuring the time it takes a new hire to ship their first change to production and treating that number as a product metric. Their time dropped from eleven days to two. I need to find out what our metric is, as it is likely poor.

Key takeaways:
1. Re-evaluate whether the order service needs event sourcing.
2. Determine the actual logging cost and explore shifting resources to tracing.
3. Pilot contract testing between the mobile team and the orders API, with an owner, perhaps Ahmed.
4. Set up the call with the Kraków team before we begin the Kafka migration.
5. Measure the time to first production change for new hires.

name: a translation from English to German
input: The new office opened on Monday, and most of the team spent the first morning arguing about desks. The building is an old printing works near the canal, with high ceilings, brick walls and windows that let in far more light than the old place ever did. The downside is the noise. Sound travels across the open floor in a way that nobody expected, and by lunchtime two people had already asked whether we could buy more headphones. Facilities have promised acoustic panels by the end of the month, but until then the meeting rooms will be in high demand. Please book them through the calendar instead of simply walking in, even for short calls, because three teams now share the space. The kitchen is larger, the coffee machine is new, and there is finally a proper place to lock bicycles in the courtyard. Parking is harder. There are only twelve spaces, and they are reserved for people with disabilities and for visitors. The nearest tram stop is five minutes away, and the company will refund monthly tickets for anyone who switches from driving. If you have any problems with access cards, ask at reception rather than holding the door for strangers.
output: Das neue Büro wurde am Montag eröffnet, und der größte Teil des Teams verbrachte den ersten Vormittag mit Diskussionen über Schreibtische. Das Gebäude ist eine alte Druckerei am Kanal, mit hohen Decken, Backsteinwänden und Fenstern, die viel mehr Licht hereinlassen als im alten Büro. Der Nachteil ist der Lärm. Geräusche tragen sich über die offene Fläche auf eine Weise, mit der niemand gerechnet hatte, und schon zur Mittagszeit fragten zwei Kolleginnen, ob wir mehr Kopfhörer kaufen könnten. Die Hausverwaltung hat Akustikpaneele bis Ende des Monats versprochen, aber bis dahin werden die Besprechungsräume sehr gefragt sein. Bitte bucht sie über den Kalender, anstatt einfach hineinzugehen, auch für kurze Gespräche, denn inzwischen teilen sich drei Teams die Fläche. Die Küche ist größer, die Kaffeemaschine ist neu, und im Innenhof gibt es endlich einen ordentlichen Platz zum Abschließen von Fahrrädern. Das Parken ist schwieriger. Es gibt nur zwölf Stellplätze, und sie sind für Menschen mit Behinderungen und für Besucher reserviert. Die nächste Straßenbahnhaltestelle ist fünf Minuten entfernt, und die Firma erstattet Monatskarten für alle, die vom Auto umsteigen. Bei Problemen mit Zugangskarten fragt bitte am Empfang, anstatt Fremden die Tür aufzuhalten.
